With strong lithe limbs and large elongated body, the gomitoad leaps from branch to branch in search of camouflaged leaf insects 
to pounce upon and feast. Living a rather fearless existence for a toad, its brightly colored body warns predators of their toxin-laden 
skin which works for most, except scavick, who can survive the lethal lunegrove toxin in small doses. Both male and female toads 
aggressively guard a single tree, wrestling with rival toads with their set of two frontal horns. Unlike most amphibians, the gomitoad 
has evolved to live in the canopy far from bodies of water. It keeps its body moist in rain water collected in leaves, and when the drier 
seasons approach, will dig divots in the tree bark to collect rain water to keep itself hydrated.
